title: Reversible field-free superconducting diode effect controlled by an antiferromagnet
authors: Filip Krizek, Kamil Olejník, Tobias Edwinson, August Jacobi, Athira Suresh, Andrej Farkaš, Jan Kraus, Vít Novák, Christoph Müller, Vojtěch Pařízek, Niclas Heinsdorf, Peter Wadley, Oliver Amin, Kevin Edmonds, Tomas Jungwirth, Libor Šmejkal, Anna Birk Hellenes, Sumit Ghosh, Michal Mazur, Dominik Kriegner, Lucas Casparis, Saulius Vaitiekėnas
abstract: The semiconductor diode, which allows current to flow preferentially in one direction, is a fundamental building block of numerous modern electronic circuits. Its superconducting analogue---the superconducting diode effect---enables directional dissipationless current flow and may provide similar functionality in future superconducting quantum circuits. Realization of such a nonreciprocal supercurrent requires broken time-reversal symmetry. At zero applied field, this has been typically associated either with intrinsic unconventional superconductivity or extrinsic spin-split electronic states induced by magnetic proximity. Here we demonstrate a field-free superconducting diode effect in conventional superconducting Al proximitized by collinear antiferromagnetic CuMnAs, whose electronic structure breaks time-reversal symmetry without generating spin splitting. By tuning the proximity effect through an insulating AlAs interlayer and correlating the reversal of the diode polarity with the reversal of the remanent Néel state, we establish that the antiferromagnet controls the superconducting diode effect. Our results show that neither spin-split bands nor net magnetization is required for a magnetically controlled field-free superconducting diode effect, extending superconducting nonreciprocity to a broader class of collinear compensated magnets.
summary: This work demonstrates a superconducting diode effect in a field-free setup using an antiferromagnetically coupled superconductor. The key finding is that the diode's directionality is controlled solely by manipulating the AFM's internal Néel state, proving that such non-reciprocity does not require net magnetization or spin-split bands. This opens a pathway for realizing superconducting quantum components using collinear compensated magnets.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate and control the superconducting diode effect (SDE) in a field-free manner, which requires breaking time-reversal symmetry.
main_result: A field-free SDE is achieved in Al proximitized by an antiferromagnet (CuMnAs), and its polarity is shown to be controlled by reversing the remanent Néel state of the AFM, without requiring spin splitting or net magnetization.
method: The study combines experimental measurements (I-V curves, magnetotransport) with theoretical calculations (DFT) to characterize the superconducting junction and its magnetic control.
model_or_system: The physical system is a heterostructure: superconducting Al, an insulating AlAs spacer, and a collinear antiferromagnetic CuMnAs layer. The mechanism relies on the AFM order breaking T-symmetry in a spin-degenerate manner.
key_observables: Diode efficiency ($\eta$), switching currents ($I_{	ext{SW}}^{+}, |I_{	ext{SW}}^{-}$), and the nonlinear resistance ($	ext{Reven}$).
important_parameters: Antiferromagnetic Néel state reversal, spacer layer thickness, and applied magnetic field strength ($H_{	ext{prep}}$).
main_assumptions: The superconducting proximity effect is modeled, and the control mechanism is assumed to be directly linked to the AFM's remanent state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the heterostructure, magnetization loops showing field-induced Néel state reversal, and I-V curves demonstrating the non-reciprocal current flow ($\eta$) that reverses upon magnetic field cycling.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the background on SDE, details the $	ext{CuMnAs/AlAs/Al}$ heterostructure, measures the SDE and its dependence on the AFM state via field preparation, and correlates this with theoretical predictions.
why_interesting: The finding that non-reciprocity can be controlled by a compensated, spin-degenerate AFM state, rather than relying on conventional spin-splitting mechanisms, expands the scope of magnetically induced superconducting phenomena relevant to quantum circuits.
